These gaps are not always sheer nothingness. A capacity that has not yet become actual is still a real capacity, though it marks an incomplete state.
If created things are willed for God's sake, this does not mean that God turns toward lower things as though He needed them.

The benefit of an act must suit the act itself. If the act is the ordering of the whole world—bringing new realities into being, forming created things, and arranging everything with the highest care—then its ultimate end cannot be less than the Necessary Being Himself. Nothing is more beautiful or more complete than He is. Someone who knows that beauty and perfection would make every action a means toward that one end, rather than seek a separate reward. Since God is the one who brings about and orders the whole, He must also be its final end. That end is for creatures to know Him so fully that the knower loses himself in what he knows.

God's appearing to creatures in complete unity is not something separate from God: an appearance wholly separate from a thing would not be its appearance at all. Just as God's knowledge and His other attributes are one with His being, so His being known by others does not add something separate to Him. His own reality is the final end of every end. — س قده
The example concerns a will that is itself effective knowledge, without a separate motive or desire following it.
The perfections that created beings gain through knowing God do not give God a new perfection; He is already complete and remains the ultimate aim. — س قده
When an image arises in our minds, desire may follow it directly, with no second act of will between them. — س قده
The definition of power is complete without adding “whether or not the agent wills.” In us, power is potential; in God, it is fully actual.
The point is that God's action is complete and His power fully actual; His action does not arise from an unresolved possibility. — س قده

Where the text says that God has no definition, we might have expected it to add, “and so no proof can establish Him.” Instead, the argument speaks of both knowing what a thing is and judging that it is, because the expression “if it has a cause” applies to both.

A complete definition contains the causes that make a thing what it is, and a complete proof contains the causes that explain why a statement about it is true. Definitions and proofs therefore share a concern with causes, as discussed earlier. The final words, “He is known through Himself,” stand where we might have expected “There is no proof of Him.”

In other works the author gives three possibilities for what has no cause. It may be clearer than anything else; it may be beyond the reach of our understanding; or it may be known through its effects. Avicenna does not discuss knowledge through effects here, because he defines wisdom as complete knowledge, whereas that route falls short of it. Nor does he dwell on our inability to know God's innermost reality, since that point is already plain.

The reality of existence can be known only through direct awareness, not through a definition. For this reason, the Necessary Being can be known only by direct illumination. Every intellect and soul, through knowing itself directly, also has some direct awareness of Him, though not of His innermost reality.

Calling this awareness a “conception” may be exact or may be a loose use of language, depending on whether we reserve “conception” and “judgment” for knowledge gained through ideas. The word may instead refer to the ordinary, self-evident idea of existence. When direct knowledge is said to come first, its priority means that what is known is more evident and known through itself.

So when Avicenna says that God is conceived and known through Himself, he means that beings free from matter have direct awareness of Him, not that they comprehend His innermost reality. They know Him through their awareness of themselves, because dependent beings can be understood only through their causes. This is one meaning of the saying, “I have never seen anything without seeing God before it.”
Things receive what they need according to their capacity, as valleys fill with water in proportion to their size.
The argument is aimed at Muʿtazilites, who accept that pointless action is wrong; Ashʿarites do not accept this moral rule.
Jurists use the purpose of a law, such as deterring murder, when they infer rulings in cases not explicitly settled by scripture. — س قده
An act is pointless when it is the sort of deliberate act normally done for a reason, but no reason is present.

There are two kinds of final end to consider. The first is nearness to God, the highest end of all and the goal of every longing. Reaching it involves passing through the gate of all gates: the complete human being, called the gate to God. This will come to pass, for God's giving does not cease, His words do not run out, and matter does not simply vanish. Everything moves toward the human level and comes to its threshold; other things are created for the sake of humanity. The human being, in turn, travels toward God and is created for His sake. The second kind of end is the fulfillment proper to each thing under one of God's beautiful names.

Things reach that end as well. All God's names are beautiful and all His attributes are exalted; things finally pass into the source of enduring life. This may help explain the reported saying, ‘Do not set me above Jonah son of Matthew,’ whose account of ascent differs from that of the Prophet. From this point of view, philosophers have said that even lives cut short reach their natural end and that what sounds out of tune has its place in the larger harmony. This shows why it is wrong to say that God destroys things before they can reach any fulfillment.
“Benefit” can be something that follows an act or something found during it, such as finding treasure while digging a well for water.
The author says the body has many distinct powers. For example, each muscle has its own powers of movement, and each organ has its own nutritive power.
All beings return to God through the perfect human being, who stands at the gate of divine unity. The return of the whole is like the return of each individual.

The Ashʿarites sometimes explain this through kasb, or “acquisition”: God creates an action when a person firmly intends it, and that is enough to make commands, reward, and punishment meaningful. They compare it to someone carrying a heavy load while another person merely places a hand beneath it. The author says this excuse is worse than the claim it is meant to defend. — س قده

It is said that the judge ʿAbd al-Jabbār entered the home of the vizier Ibn ʿAbbād and saw the theologian Abū Isḥāq al-Isfarāʾīnī there. The judge said, “Glory be to God, who is above indecency.” The theologian replied, “Glory be to God, in whose kingdom nothing happens except what He wills.” — س قده

The Qur'an asks, “Are many separate lords better, or God, the One who prevails?” A report from the Prophet calls the Qadariyya—the people who deny God’s decree—the Zoroastrians of this community. Each side accused the other of holding this view.

This includes Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Tusi, as cited earlier. In this account, God creates a person’s power and will; these then bring about the action. God is the distant cause, and the person the immediate cause. The people firmly grounded in knowledge describe God as near in His distance and far in His nearness. Unlike the Muʿtazilites, al-Tusi also holds that an effect continues to depend on its cause in order to exist.

God does not will evil directly or for its own sake. It follows indirectly from a good that He wills. The terms “will,” “approval,” “love,” and “delight” are used here with a particular technical distinction. — س قده

The third view moves from multiplicity within unity; the fourth moves from unity within multiplicity. In the third, an action depends both on its immediate cause and, through that cause, on the cause behind it. These are ordered relations, so one does not cancel the other. The First Cause wills the action to come from a willing agent, so the action occurs by choice; it does not bypass that agent’s choice. In the fourth view, God’s action is directly present through His encompassing knowledge, while the action also truly belongs to its created agent. The two views therefore do not contradict one another.

The divine reality is the enduring source and ground of all things, not a part mixed into them or a separate source standing beside them. It is present to every action, though the source has aspects that do not belong to its effects. Existence first belongs to God; created things receive existence from Him, and their essences are considered afterward. Keep these levels distinct: when we look at unity, the effect is God’s; when we look at the many created beings, their actions are theirs. This does not make God composite.

Names for limited things and actions include the conditions that limit them, such as subject, matter, time, and place. These are aspects of imperfection. What is attributed to God is their existence, without these limits. For example, if you imagine someone eating bread or drinking wine, that person and their action depend on you as the one who imagines them. The action is called eating or drinking when attributed to the person; when attributed to you, you are said to have brought the person and action into being. The author does not say that you yourself eat bread or drink wine.

The prayer “All good is in Your hands, and evil is not from You” means that evil is not affirmed as a thing in itself. The author also alludes to the Qur'anic promise that the earth and heavens will be changed, along with the one who sees and what is seen, so that evil will no longer be attributed to pure good.

These lines point to the oneness of God’s essence, attributes, and actions. A person who affirms God’s oneness must first affirm the oneness of His essence and attributes, then the oneness of His actions. The Ashʿarites claim to affirm the latter, but, in the author’s view, they do so incorrectly: they treat created beings as independent existences while denying that their actions and effects belong to them, then assign those effects to God as their place of occurrence.

The soul's unity is a true unity, but only as a reflection of God's unity. It can know divine names that point both to God's difference from creation and to His nearness to it. At its lower level, the soul has the powers of bodily nature; at its higher level, it has the qualities of spiritual beings. Through all these levels it remains the one source of its powers.

Because the soul is God's reflection and representative, it bears, in its own limited way, something of the qualities of the One it represents. It therefore has a level of hidden unity, where its many powers are gathered in a higher and undivided way. It also has a level of outward expression, where one soul acts through many powers without leaving its higher level behind.

The note connects this with the two blasts of the trumpet. At the first, which brings death, the soul's powers cease to shine separately through the scattered organs of the body. At the second, which brings renewed life, those powers rise in another form. They no longer depend on bodily matter for their existence; they are gathered into one simple life through the soul itself. At the first blast their separate modes of existence pass away. At the second they endure after that passing, raised together in a higher existence.

The difficulty comes from tracing all things to God’s knowledge of the most complete order, which is identical with His essence, and from holding that an effect cannot be separated from its cause. Calling this knowledge “will” or “an attribute of action” rather than “an attribute of essence” does not resolve the problem.

Decree is God’s active knowledge; what is decreed is what He knows. Each has a property that the other does not. We may say that God’s knowledge of all things is one, but we cannot say that all the things He knows are one.

The author does not deny that decree differs from what is decreed, or that God’s prior knowledge differs from the things known. He questions whether the required contentment concerns decree in that sense. Since approval and disapproval apply to the same things, they concern the created event, not prior knowledge. The discussion therefore distinguishes approving disbelief as an event decreed by God from approving it as disbelief. — ط مد ظله

The earlier statement that acceptance of what is decreed comes down to acceptance of the decree assumes that “decree” means the act of decreeing. But that is not the meaning used by the thinkers under discussion. For them, divine decree means the existence of the forms of things at an earlier level. On this reading, they can approve of things in that prior state while rejecting their condition in this world. In their view, earthly existence is mixed with dark matter, extension, and constant change. It also contains things that are plainly blameworthy.

The objection need not be answered through such fine distinctions, however. Approval and disapproval each have their own object. If someone asks how anything that exists can be disapproved of when existence itself is good, the answer is that disapproval of a shameful thing concerns its particular nature—or, more precisely, the lack of good found in it—not existence as such.

The statement can also cover the decree as it appears in the world, a use associated with Mīr Dāmād. If “decree” is taken broadly enough to include destiny, then the actual existence of things falls within it. Their existence can be approved insofar as they are lights and objects of knowledge, turned towards God. They can also be approved as faint expressions of higher realities, wholly dependent on those realities.

Whatever meaning we give to divine decree, it is an attribute of God, who decrees. If it means His essential knowledge, it is an attribute of essence. If it means the existence of created events as related to Him and subject to His judgment, it is an attribute of action. — ط مد ظله

Al-Tusi’s phrase “not from this point of view” refers to created qualities and actions under the names that relate them to their subjects. Heat and cold, for example, are attributed to God as existences He creates, but as heat and cold they belong to fire and ice. God is not Himself hot or cold. The author’s three answers are each correct in a different respect. — ط مد ظله
This clarifies how the thing decreed may be disapproved while its divine source is not. The divine names behind things considered evil are themselves beautiful.
The Qur'an does not say, “Because You led me astray.” It does quote Satan as saying, “Because You made me err,” but that does not support the claim being made here.
The parallel argument applies to God’s will for events that arise in time: if God knew and willed such an event, it would have to be eternal; if He did not, it could not come into being. — س قده

The author may have in mind his later answer: divine knowledge applies to things as they are. So it applies to a chosen action precisely as something that comes from a person’s power and choice. — ط مد ظله

In Tajrīd al-iʿtiqād, al-Tusi says knowledge “follows” what it knows in the sense that the two must correspond. In the mystical account, knowledge follows things in their particular form and coloring, because knowledge itself is light without color. — س قده

This is enough to make the action voluntary. A voluntary action is one preceded by choice; choice itself need not be preceded by another choice. God’s decree contains both the person’s power, will, and choice, and the action that follows them. Just as your existence is truly yours even though God gives it, your choice is truly yours. To deny the qualities and effects of something while affirming the thing itself would be strange.

One answer is that commands and prohibitions are meant to bring about a deeper understanding and state of being, not merely to inform us. Another is that although God gives power for human actions, people also act by their own power, as already explained.
“Obligatory” here means that failing to do it would merit blame. This differs from “necessary” as opposed to possible or impossible, which is the sense that would rule out power. — س قده
The first claim allows for intermediary causes and for the two attributions to differ. The second denies this.

Strictly speaking, it is strange to call a will “human” if the person does not will it. The objection means that this account severs the connection between a person and their will, and more broadly between causes and their effects, leaving actions to follow only from God’s custom. — ط مد ظله
Since even a compelled agent may act with some will, “choice” would be a more precise word here than “will.” — ط مد ظله

This is what distinguishes the author’s possible answer from his teacher’s. The teacher says that one act of will is inherently prior to the next, and so on. But inherent earlier and later parts belong only to extended things, not to one simple state of the soul.

This argument is compelling if essences are primary, as the teacher holds, or if individual examples of one kind are considered alike. The author’s view is that existence is primary and graded: it is one reality in different degrees, so one degree may cause another. He also allows that members of one kind can differ, with some material and others immaterial.

“Decree” may refer to the intellectual images in the First Intellect, while “measure” refers to the impressions in the souls of the heavens. It may also mean the First Intellect itself, or the first intellectual act of knowing. — س قده

Chance is an event such as a falling stone striking Zayd as his will carries him beneath it. It is chance when judged from a limited perspective. From the perspective of all causes and the complete order, it is necessary. Possibility is likewise a feature of an essence considered by itself; in relation to existence and its cause, the event is necessary. Avicenna does not discuss forced causes here, since what forces something acts either by nature or by will.

“The first simple arrangement” is close to the ordinary meaning of decree. It is simple in two ways: all things exist through one simple existence, and each image there exists in a simple form, without the multiplicity found in the records of destiny. — س قده

Read “as though it necessarily produced.” The phrase “as though” is added because the gathering of causes is an abstract relation. Their existence is one; the meeting of their concepts gives rise to the specific forms and settings found in the records of destiny.

Some thinkers exclude these existences—which others count as forms of knowledge—from the levels of knowledge. The author therefore expands and completes his explanation through the Tablet of Destiny. — س قده

First, divine oneness knows its own essence; then it considers other things. For philosophers who affirm images in God, this second act is the forms of other things in His essence. Since divine knowledge is active and brings about what it knows, it is also called power. “The second knowledge followed” explains how the first knowledge gives rise to the second. — س قده

The note describes two stages of multiplicity: first, knowledge becomes detailed as it unfolds from its original unity; then the contents of knowledge become many as they are written in the tablet. The letters on paper were once one in the wet ink on the tip of the reed pen. The “Lote Tree” may also refer to the universal soul, the forms impressed upon it, or the great intermediate realm of divine names and attributes. — س قده

Divine agency has levels. The phrase about God’s beautiful names may explain the earlier point: in the mystical tradition, the divine names are like the archetypes or “lords” of kinds in Illuminationist philosophy. Created kinds are manifestations of those names.

“Heart” and “breast” are technical terms here. The breast can mean the imagination, which holds images that reflect subtle truths from the world of unity; an expanded breast is a luminous imagination. A constricted breast can mean a dark imagination that multiplies things into separate forms. — س قده

Without these changing records, there would be no successive beings or chain of events. Only fixed immaterial beings would exist in a vertical order. Some mystics therefore say that a complete world requires the creation of an imperfect world as well.

This account may seem difficult to reconcile with the view that heavenly bodies do not change inwardly. One way to understand it is that their movements and positions carry universal patterns that include their consequences. A heavenly soul can know the rules that connect certain movements with certain earthly events, and infer what follows as conditions change. A prophet or saint connected to such a soul may see some of these forms, but no human being knows every consequence of every heavenly movement. What is seen may therefore change or be incomplete. — س قده

The hidden knowledge comprehends all particulars, their causes, and whatever might prevent them. The knowledge taught to angels and messengers includes broad rules and some particulars. This does not conflict with the claim that God alone knows the unseen: any knowledge they receive comes through His power and knowledge. — س قده

Avicenna’s phrase “a soul spread through the world of coming-to-be and decay” is unclear. It might mean the collective of individual souls, an active source behind them, or a soul associated with an unchanging heavenly body. If the last, that soul may overlap with what mystics call the pole or helper of the world. The prophetic and saintly souls, which the earth is never without, must also be connected to the heavenly soul in their knowledge and action. The author’s wording may be an indirect way of referring to them. — س قده

This proposed soul is not a third option in addition to the two Avicenna listed. The preferred option is a heavenly soul. The author later argues that such a soul is not higher in every respect and may respond to some earthly events.
The cause’s knowledge is active: what it knows brings about what it knows.

Prayer and asking are also causes of our happiness because they remind us of God. God told Moses to ask Him for everything, even salt for his food. A Persian verse says: “Even if you pray and I do not grant your wish, / what I seek from you is your pleading.” If you ask for bodily health and do not receive it, the All-Merciful may know that your soul needs another kind of health. The soul begins as a simple capacity; what makes a thing fully itself is its form. There is no comparison between having the divine names and attributes become the form of your soul, and having passing worldly things become its form. Another verse says: “A house is not a heart if it holds / cattle, donkeys, fields, and property.”
The person’s will is contained within God’s effective will: the person gives up what they want for what God wants. God “does what He wills and chooses what He wants.”

The prayer can be known to God because the person intends to make it. But it does not follow that the person knows God’s full knowledge: another known cause may prevent the request from being granted.
All the forms of things in God’s realm come from Him. A maker who makes their own tools does not need anything outside themselves. — س قده
The first view described here belongs to the philosophers in Aristotle’s school; the second is the Illuminationist view. — س قده

The earthly causes form a chain beneath the chain of heavenly causes. When heavenly souls know the first causes, they can also know the later effects, since knowledge of a cause can lead to knowledge of its effect.

Heavenly souls are said to have the power to act and to perceive particular meanings and images, as well as universals and separate intellects. The discussion here concerns their knowledge of particulars. — س قده

“Not a passing desire” means that the will is decisive. Desire may become a firm resolve and then a settled decision, but a new obstacle can still prevent action. A will that is a complete cause does not fail to bring about its action. Avicenna says that particular events have natural or voluntary causes, and treats forced action as ultimately arising from one of these.
A heavenly soul may know a particular directly, through the common sense that gathers sensory impressions, or through something that reaches a direct perceiver. — س قده
The event is not caused only by natural causes. It may arise from an active conception and knowledge in the heavenly source. — س قده

“But” here adds a further point rather than correcting what came before. The recipient’s capacities and needs also contribute to what comes into being, though the true creative power belongs to the higher causes.

Avicenna may mean that the heavens are not affected by earthly things simply as earthly things. He may allow an effect from a higher earthly reality, such as the human being, who bears the greatest divine trust and for whose sake other things were created. — س قده

This discussion relies on older philosophical and physical assumptions: moving celestial spheres with individual souls, four elements, and other ideas later overturned by modern science. Setting those assumptions aside, the author’s general account can be restated in terms of three ordered worlds: matter, imagination, and immaterial intellect. Material events depend on the imaginal world, which in turn depends on intellect. A person who prays with persistence may become connected to the causes of what they need in the imaginal and intellectual worlds, and so affect material events. This can also explain miracles. Shared disasters such as floods and earthquakes may be understood through the unity of the whole world: the state of one part affects the rest, as illness in one organ disturbs the body. Human society also has a natural purpose and a divinely given way of life. Widespread injustice and wrongdoing can therefore disturb the larger order, which responds through consequences appropriate to the situation. — ط مد ظله

The response need not mean that the heavenly soul first learns of the event after it happens. It can mean that an awareness arising with the event completes its earlier awareness of the causes. We can know that we will move and also perceive the movement as it happens.
“Under Our eyes” refers to the heavenly souls; “by Our revelation” refers to the conceptions they receive.
The words “I hear and see” refer to God’s knowledge of particular events through the level of the heavenly souls. — س قده

Even if one questions the separate archetypes, this does not rule out forms of material things and their effects at higher levels. The imaginal world contains forms suited to material things, and the intellectual world contains what is in the imaginal world, each according to its own level. — ط مد ظله

Avicenna accepts particular images in the souls of the heavens and universal images in the intellects above them. But this alone does not establish that the real essences of things exist in those worlds. Philosophers in Aristotle’s school often treat the images as accidents or qualities. They also regard it as impossible for members of one kind to be substances in one world and accidents in another. Even the Illuminationist who affirms both luminous archetypes and suspended images, the author says, did not make clear whether the luminous forms are the archetypes of natural kinds or merely similar to them.
This is generally true, though movement in place, changes in quality, changes in quantity, and other processes also contribute to life.

Strictly speaking, pure existence is not an attribute added to God alongside knowledge, power, and life. The word “attribute” is used either by analogy or to refer to the concept without considering what it describes. The author’s point is that God is pure existence, without an essence or partner. “One” means that He has no partner of any kind. — س قده

The principles that existence is primary and one in different degrees do not allow us to treat existence as a quality in God like knowledge, power, or life. Pure existence corresponds to the concepts of essence and identity. Proofs for God’s essence are also proofs for pure existence. Knowledge and power, though identical with God in reality, have different meanings and are established after His essence.
The relational aspect is included in this definition of life because it describes the two results of life: perception and action. Life itself remains a real, essential attribute.
The question is what makes a body alive, not what makes it a body. — س قده
This applies to God and separate immaterial substances. But prime matter and bodies that remain connected to matter do not have this kind of existence.

These theologians believe that reason alone cannot establish life as an attribute of God. They rely on scripture, since they think life is a bodily quality arising from a physical mixture, while God is above bodies and mixtures. “Then” marks a shift to the next point. — س قده
